As time goes on in the graph, there are more earthquakes of lesser magnitude. There are also fewer earthquakes above a magnitude of 7 in the last 40 years. That being said, recent earthquakes seem to have more potential for high death tolls. The question for these trends is, why?

Before 1960, seismometers may have just not been sensitive enough to detect an earthquake with a magnitude smaller than 5. However, there is also a trend for a decrease in high magnitude earthquakes. It appears that in the last 120 years, there have been a trend for smaller, more frequent earthquakes in turkey, indicating more frequent releases of energy in the crust. In my opinion, this graph shows how many documents can give more insight than what is obvious at a glance.

raw_comment: The graph Earthquakes talks about the number of deaths in major earthquakes since 1900. The graph is represented in circles instead of bars and dots. This relates to my community because it makes me wonder if there’s anything we can do to either prevent earthquakes and, or, help the people that have to deal with earthquakes as a recurring thing in their lives. I would name this graph: “Magnitude: Impact or Livelyhood?”

Turkey, Syria, and other countries in the Middle East sit on the Anatolian fault line, which is notorious for causing infrequent but strong tremors. This, paired with the high population density, and large amounts of impoverished people living in slums with unstable structures, especially near the Syrian border due to a large number of refugees, which creates a ticking time bomb.  This can be seen by the fact that all the high-magnitude earthquakes with high death tolls are located in the Middle East. This is also interesting to note how, despite these countries may not have the highest magnitude (namely the 1988 Armenian quake) but have disproportionally larger death tolls than other quakes of that magnitude. 
I wonder where the high magnitude quakes with low death tolls are centered. I hypothesize around the center of Turkey where there is less population density. 
This directly affects the community of people I interact with because I have a close friend who lives in Turkey who, thankfully, neither she nor her family was hurt, but her dad did lose his source of income because the building he worked in was destroyed. Turkey's government needs to be more prepared with better infrastructure in these high-population-density cities and a plan of action for immediate relief and recovery after a disaster like this.

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I notice that overall there is a moderate correlation, and over the years there was a decrease. From 1900-1960 the deaths were fairly linear, most deaths falling between a magnitude of 6-7. Within this time frame, the largest amount of estimated deaths were in 1939 Turkey, with a magnitude of 7.7. After 1960, there were less earthquakes of higher magnitudes but more clusters. I imagine this is due to the fact that the higher magnitude earthquakes caused more deaths, making clusters less possible compared to a lot of smaller earthquakes occurring around the same time. I also noticed that out of the 4 major earthquakes that are larger circles, Turkey was affected by most (3/4). 
2) What do you wonder?
After the 2000's there is an increase in magnitude after having a downward trend for a period of time prior, so I wonder if we will ever see an earthquake that surpasses the magnitude and/or deaths of Turkey, 1939. 
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
Many in my community have not experienced earthquakes, but the graph can relate to us as we can work towards helping those who do have to deal with these disasters by bringing awareness and providing aid.
4) What’s going on in this graph?
The graph depicts deaths in major earthquakes since 1900 around Turkey and northern Syria. My headline for it would be "Earthquakes Shatter Lives Across Turkey and Syria"

1) I noticed that from 1900 to 2023 the magnitude of the earthquake fluctuated years. From 1960 to 2023, more earthquakes have been occurring with magnitudes of all ranges from 4 to 7.8. Governments from all over the world need to open their eyes and realize that climate change is real and our environment is (basically) having enough of us. 

4) BEFORE Turkey and Syria 2023: How many Earthquakes did they have?

What do you notice?
I have noticed that Turkey, Syria, and Armenia are quite vulnerable to earthquakes of all sizes, but they are especially susceptible to those with devastating magnitudes and enormous numbers of fatalities. The most devastating earthquake happened in 1939 in Turkey, where an estimated 32,000+ people died. It had the greatest Magnitude of any earthquake and occurred in Turkey and Syria.

What do you wonder?
Regarding the locations of these large earthquakes and the significance of the association between "areas and death" and "areas and magnitude," I wonder if the earthquake's epicenter has a higher impact on the death toll than the magnitude alone.

How does this relate to you and your community?

1.  The most hazardous earthquakes, according to my observation, occurred in Turkey, Armenia, and Syria, with Turkey having an incredible three main quakes with magnitudes above 7. I also notice that there have been more earthquakes recently, with the number of earthquakes doubling after 1960 when they went from being very strong to being moderately weak. Since some earthquakes with magnitudes close to 8 have hardly any fatalities, the graph disproves the common belief that the higher the magnitude, the more deaths.

2. First, I'm curious as to why there have been twice as many earthquakes since 1960. Is this a result of rising populations or unstable building designs that have been made taller in many parts of the world? A change in our environment and the Earth's composition, which makes it simpler for these occurrences to recur, could also be blamed for the rise in smaller earthquakes below the magnitude of 5.

3. In New Jersey, I have never experienced an earthquake, and they are not at all common in this region. However, I believe that in the event of an earthquake, the number of fatalities would be relatively low given the lack of tall buildings in the area where I live. Unlike our neighboring state New York, where a single building collapsing could result in a significant number of fatalities.

4.  "The Effect of Earth's Deadliest Temper Tantrums"

Living near a bay puts my community at a higher risk for water natural disasters.

raw_comment:
Turkey Earthquakes: Why are so many people still dying?
I notice that the higher the magnitude earthquake in Turkey, the higher the number of people who died rises as well. For example, in 1999 the 7.6 magnitude earthquake had roughly 17000 people die whereas in 2023 the 7.8 magnitude earthquake had roughly 20000 people die. I wonder why there was an anomaly in 1988 where the 6.8 magnitude earthquake had roughly 25000 people die. I just find it interesting that this specific earthquake had killed so many more people than the 7.6 magnitude earthquake and the 7.8 magnitude one. Also, I am curious as to why, with the more modern technology, so many more people had passed in more recent years. Yes, an earthquake can kill many, but I'm surprised with better technology and earlier warnings, how more people didn't try to get to better grounds, etc. This relates to my community and I because where I am from, the west side of Washington, there are many active volcanoes in our area. The Mount Saint Helen's eruption had killed many in 1980 and Mount Rainier is said to be long overdue for its eruption. In this graph you can see the different sized circles on a graph with years from 1900 on where they mark how many people died in a specific earthquake.
